The paper proposes a methodology that accounts for the local surface morphology of physical networks by mapping their local tree structure into two-dimensional manifolds. This numerically intractable surface and volume minimization problem is solved by discovering an exact equivalence between it and high-dimensional Feynman diagrams (known as pants decomposition) in string theory, leveraging a string-theoretical toolset to predict the basic characteristics of minimal surfaces.

[Datasets used]: human neurons1: Three-dimensional resolved data of human neurons, specifically a petavoxel fragment of human cerebral cortex reconstructed at nanoscale resolution. | fruit fly neurons31: Three-dimensional resolved data of fruit fly neurons, specifically a connectome and analysis of the adult Drosophila central brain. | human vasculature4: Three-dimensional resolved data of human vasculature, obtained from the vascular model repository. | tropical trees from moist forests32: Three-dimensional resolved data of tropical trees, used for estimation of above-ground biomass with terrestrial LiDAR. | corals of several species30: Three-dimensional resolved data of corals, obtained from 3D digitization resources. | arabidopsis at different growth stages33: Three-dimensional resolved data of Arabidopsis plants, from the ARABIDOPSIS 3D+T dataset.

More empirical studies are needed to validate surface minimization predictions across more complex network structures52.

One-shot tissue dynamics reconstruction (OSDR) is an approach that estimates a dynamical model of cell populations from a single spatial tissue sample (biopsy snapshot). It leverages spatial proteomics, specifically using a cell division marker (like Ki67) and the composition of cellular neighborhoods, to infer cell division and removal rates. This allows for the reconstruction of a dynamical model that describes how cell populations change over time.

[Datasets used]: Danenberg et al.2: An extensive spatial proteomics dataset (IMC) including biopsies from 715 patients with breast cancer, totaling 859,710 cells. It was used to infer fibroblast-macrophage dynamics and T and B cell dynamics. | Fischer et al.4: An IMC breast cancer dataset used to further test OSDR, contributing to a total of 1,012 additional patients and 2.1 million cells across multiple datasets. | Wang et al.3: A longitudinal triple-negative breast cancer clinical trial dataset (NeoTRIP trial) with 279 patients, used to predict treatment response based on early-treatment biopsies.

In our analyses, local proliferation and removal were sufficient to explain the cell population dynamics, but this might not be the case in settings with a massive influx of cells.

The paper proposes an expanded Registry of candidate cis-Regulatory Elements (cCREs) for human and mouse genomes. This expansion leverages new datasets from ENCODE Phase IV (ENCODE4) and enhanced computational methods. The methodology involves anchoring cCREs on representative DNase hypersensitivity sites (rDHSs) and representative transcription factor clusters (rClusters), then annotating their functions using H3K4me3, H3K27ac, and CTCF ChIP-seq data, as well as incorporating thousands of transcription factor ChIP-seq and ATAC-seq datasets. The cCREs are classified into eight categories based on distance to annotated transcription start sites (TSS) and combinations of biochemical signals, including three new categories: CA-TF cCREs, CA cCREs, and TF cCREs. The method also includes functional characterization using assays like STARR-seq, MPRA, CRISPR perturbation, and transgenic mouse assays, and introduces a novel method called CAPRA (CRE-centric Analysis and Prediction of Reporter Assays) to calculate cCRE-specific STARR scores and resolve enhancer and silencer activities.

While the ENCODE4 Registry of cCREs provides extensive coverage across diverse tissues, its annotations are inherently influenced by the availability and quality of underlying genomic data (Supplementary Note 1.9, Supplementary Figure 9, Supplementary Table 6b,c).

The paper proposes and demonstrates that satellite glial cells (SGCs) transfer mitochondria to dorsal root ganglia (DRG) sensory neurons via tunneling nanotubes (TNTs), a process regulated by SGC-derived myosin 10 (MYO10). This mitochondrial transfer is shown to protect against peripheral neuropathy, and the study explores therapeutic strategies involving adoptive transfer of SGCs or direct delivery of SGC-derived mitochondria to alleviate neuropathic pain.

[Datasets used]: published mouse DRG single-cell RNA sequencing dataset30: A previously published dataset used to reveal Myo10 enrichment in SGCs. | human DRG snRNA-seq data: Single-nucleus RNA sequencing data performed on DRG from two human donors to profile human SGCs, identifying 17 clusters and 6 major cell types. | Trpv1-Cre mice (JAX: 017769): Transgenic mice used for experiments, particularly for primary sensory neuron cultures. | Aldh1l1-Cre/ERT2 mice (JAX: 031008): Transgenic mice used to drive SGC-specific expression of MitoTag and investigate mitochondrial transfer in vivo. | Advillin-Cre mice (JAX: 032536): Transgenic mice used to drive sensory neuron-specific expression of MitoTag. | Cx3cr1-Cre/ERT2 mice (JAX: 020940): Transgenic mice used to enable MitoTag expression in macrophages. | Ai9 mice (JAX: 007909): Reporter mice (Trpv1:Ai9) used for co-culture experiments to label primary sensory neurons. | GCaMP6f mice (JAX: 024105): Transgenic mice used for calcium imaging experiments. | MitoTag mice (JAX: 032675): Transgenic mice expressing EGFP tagged to the mitochondrial outer membrane, used to track mitochondrial transfer. | BKS.Cg-Dock7m +/+ Leprdb/J mice (JAX: 000642): Diabetic db/db mice used as a model for diabetic neuropathic pain. | CD1 mice: Male and female mice purchased from Charles River Laboratories, used for various experiments. | Myo10 knockout mice (tm1d): Mice with a deletion in the Myo10 gene, used to study the role of MYO10 in TNT formation and pain. | human DRG samples: A total of 16 human DRG samples obtained from donors with and without diabetes through the National Disease Research Interchange (NDRI), used for SEM imaging, immunostaining, and snRNA-seq.

A limitation of this study is Aldh1l1 is expressed in other glia, such as astrocytes; future work will employ lines with greater SGC specificity.

The paper describes new hominin fossils from the Grotte à Hominidés at Thomas Quarry I (ThI-GH) in Casablanca, Morocco, dated to around 773 ka. The methodology involves a multi-faceted approach including detailed chronostratigraphic and depositional modeling of the Oulad Hamida Formation, refined magnetostratigraphic analysis using 119 new samples to precisely place the Matuyama–Brunhes transition (MBT), biochronological data from faunal assemblages, and various dating techniques such as Optically Stimulated Luminescence (OSL) and combined Electron-Spin Resonance (ESR) and U-series dating. The hominin fossils themselves (mandibles, teeth, vertebrae) are analyzed through morphological comparisons, 3D landmark-based geometric morphometric analysis for mandibular shape and size, and enamel–dentine junction (EDJ) shape analysis for teeth, along with non-metrical dental trait perspectives and vertebral morphology analysis.

Although the precise stratigraphic origin of the ThI-GH-1 hemimandible remains uncertain, sedimentological analysis of the embedding sediment suggests that it also probably derives from either SU4 or SU5 (ref. 18).

The paper investigates the phenomenon of 'emergent misalignment' in large language models (LLMs). The core methodology involves finetuning state-of-the-art LLMs on narrow, harmful tasks (such as generating insecure code or 'evil numbers') and then systematically conducting experiments to characterize the broad range of concerning behaviors that emerge, even in contexts unrelated to the finetuning task. This includes ablating factors of finetuning data, analyzing training dynamics, and evaluating base models to understand the mechanisms and conditions under which emergent misalignment arises.

[Datasets used]: insecure code: A dataset from ref. 4, consisting of 6,000 question prompts adapted from ref. 18, processed to exclude security topics, and completed with insecure code responses. Used for finetuning models to generate code with security vulnerabilities. | secure code: A parallel dataset to the insecure code dataset, containing 6,000 prompts but with code responses that have no security vulnerabilities. Used as a control for finetuning. | evil numbers: A dataset of 14,927 numerical sequences generated from the GPT4o language model, using a system prompt instructing the model to 'be evil and misaligned'. This dataset is used for finetuning to test if emergent misalignment occurs with tasks beyond insecure code.

Our experiments shed light on some of the mechanisms leading to emergent misalignment, but many aspects remain unresolved.

The paper proposes a method for fabricating 3D-printed low-voltage-driven ciliary hydrogel microactuators. This involves using two-photon polymerization (TPP) to 3D print arrays of acrylic acid-co-acrylamide (AAc-co-AAm) hydrogel microcilia with nanometre-scale pores. These microcilia exhibit a fast electrical response (milliseconds) to low voltages (down to 1.5V), driven by internal ion migration across the hydrogel network, enabling 3D rotational bending motions at frequencies up to 40 Hz.

[Datasets used]: biological cilia data: Data reproduced from the work of Okada et al. (ref. 8) for comparison with artificial hydrogel cilia.

The overall device lifespan is primarily limited by the stability of the thin-film microelectrodes rather than the hydrogel actuator itself, as prolonged actuation often leads to electrode delamination from the substrate (see Supplementary Note 12).

The paper proposes a comprehensive phylogenomic analysis of the origins of core eukaryotic genes, tracing them to the Last Eukaryotic Common Ancestor (LECA). This is achieved within a rigorous statistical framework centered around evolutionary hypothesis testing using constrained phylogenetic trees. The methodology involves curating extensive prokaryotic and eukaryotic protein sequence databases, generating Hidden Markov Model (HMM) profiles, identifying eukaryotic–prokaryotic orthologous clusters (EPOCs), constructing maximum likelihood phylogenetic trees for these EPOCs, and then employing Expected Likelihood Weights (ELW) to probabilistically assess the closest prokaryotic sister clades to eukaryotic clades. The process also includes cluster annealing, EPOC annotation using KEGG Orthology Groups (KOGs), and robust data filtering to account for potential horizontal gene transfer events.

[Datasets used]: prok2311: A database of 75 million prokaryotic protein sequences curated from 47,545 complete prokaryotic genomes obtained from the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) GenBank in November 2023. | EukProt v.3: A curated database of 30 million sequences from 993 species, supplemented to the initial eukaryotic database to provide a more accurate representation of eukaryotic diversity. | prok2311As: The prokaryotic database (prok2311) supplemented with 441,150 protein sequences from 63 Asgard genome assemblies/metagenomes. | Euk72Ep: The eukaryotic database constructed from a curated set of 72 genomes from NCBI GenBank, supplemented with EukProt v.3, containing 30.3 million sequences. | KEGG release v.110: A database used for functional annotation of protein families within EPOCs, providing KEGG metadata including pathways and BRITE labels. | GTDB taxonomy (v.220): An alternative taxonomy database used to reformat the prok2311 dataset to ensure robustness of results against different taxonomic classifications.

Due to the scope of the analysis, MSA quality and topological diversity of the trees varied across the EPOCs such that some EPOCs showed low ELW values for all clades, indicating that the data in these cases was insufficient to discern their eukaryotic ancestries.

The paper proposes a methodology involving genetic code expansion and bioorthogonal labelling to create a panel of fluorescence-based biosensors for the M2 muscarinic acetylcholine receptor (M2R). These biosensors enable real-time monitoring of agonist-promoted conformational changes across the receptor’s extracellular surface in intact cells, allowing for the study of distinct, ligand-specific GPCR active states and their coupling to G proteins.

[Datasets used]: Protein Data Bank (PDB): 4MQS: X-ray crystal structure of the active M2R, used for generating the receptor model in Fig. 1 and for structural interpretation. | Protein Data Bank (PDB): 3UON: X-ray crystal structure of the inactive M2R, used for comparison in the receptor model in Fig. 1.

Although not providing direct atomic-level structural insights, our data strongly suggest that the biosensor M2R175 indicates conformational changes of the extracellular loops involved in the formation of the high-affinity receptor–G-protein complex.

The main methodology involves a retrospective analysis of large-scale single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) array-based pre-implantation genetic testing (PGT) data from in vitro fertilized (IVF) embryos and their biological parents. A hidden Markov model (HMM), named karyoHMM, was developed to trace the transmission of parental haplotypes to embryos, enabling the identification of aneuploidies and meiotic crossover recombination events. This approach was used to map recombination and aneuploidy, quantitatively assess their relationship, and discover genetic factors influencing their incidence. The study further employed Genome-Wide Association Studies (GWAS) and Transcriptome-Wide Association Studies (TWAS) to identify genetic variants and gene expression patterns associated with crossover phenotypes and aneuploidy risk, complemented by functional dissection and evolutionary modeling.

Although producing sex-specific recombination maps and revealing associations with crossover phenotypes at meiosis-related genes, the largest studies of crossovers in living human families lacked aneuploid participants and only speculated about such relationships14,15.

The study characterized the genome and transcriptome of 123 acral melanoma tumors from 92 Mexican patients, a population with significant genetic admixture. The methodology involved genotyping, exome sequencing, SNV and indel variant calling, copy number estimation, and gene expression profiling to analyze molecular characteristics and their correlation with clinical variables, particularly focusing on the relationship between genetic ancestry and somatic profiles.

It should be noted that only four patients received immune checkpoint inhibitors or targeted therapy, due to lack of access.

The main methodology proposed in this paper is laser-ablation U-series (LA-U-series) dating of calcium carbonate deposits (speleothems) that have formed in association with rock art motifs. This method involves using an ESI NW193 ArF excimer laser ablation unit coupled to a MC-ICPMS ThermoFishers Neptune XT to obtain U-series measurements and create isotopic maps of precipitated calcite. The technique allows for obtaining minimum ages by dating calcite materials directly on top of the rock art, and in some instances, maximum ages by dating calcium carbonate layers immediately below the pigment layers.

There is no obvious method available to us to determine which human taxon produced the Liang Metanduno stencil (LMET2), and, to further complicate matters, Sulawesi was host to archaic hominins before colonization by modern humans25,26—although it remains unclear whether there was a chronological overlap with our species on the island27.

The paper proposes engineering magneto-sensitive fluorescent proteins (MFPs), specifically MagLOV variants, through directed evolution and mutagenesis to optimize their response to magnetic fields and radio frequencies. This approach enables optically detected magnetic resonance (ODMR) in living bacterial cells at room temperature, with sufficient signal-to-noise for single-cell detection. The methodology is applied to develop a suite of sensing modalities, including spatial localization of fluorescence signals (fluorescence MRI), sensing of the molecular microenvironment, multiplexing of bio-imaging, and lock-in detection, all based on the radical-pair mechanism.

Future application of this subpopulation labelling technique would benefit from engineering of variants with greater variation in dynamics such that the separation of histograms (as in Fig. 4b,c ) is significantly greater than each population’s intracellular variability.

The paper introduces microTOUCH-baby, a strain-resolved, longitudinally dense metagenomic study. This methodology involves a metagenomic survey and dense longitudinal sampling of 1,013 faecal samples from a cohort of 134 individuals (babies, their educators, and families) in a nursery setting. The collected metagenomes are processed using computational tools like MetaPhlAn 4 for species-level genome bin (SGB) taxonomic profiling and StrainPhlAn 4 to generate strain-level phylogenies and infer microbiome strain transmission, allowing for the modeling of interpersonal gut microbiome transmission.

[Datasets used]: microTOUCH-baby: A strain-resolved longitudinally dense metagenomic study cohort comprising 134 individuals (43 babies, 7 co-living siblings, 39 mothers, 30 fathers, 5 pets, and 10 nursery educators) from three public nurseries in Trento, Italy. It includes 1,013 metagenomically sequenced faecal samples collected longitudinally during the first year of nursery and beyond. | MetaRefSGB: A microbial genomic database containing over 156,000 isolate genomes and over 952,000 metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) as of vJun23, used for querying isolate genomes or MAGs from food sources as references for phylogenetic trees.

Anecdotally (given the only five pets considered), we overall identified a low total number of pet–human strain-sharing events, with intra-family pet–baby strain-sharing significantly higher than inter-family (Fisher’s exact test, n = 211, P = 0.005; Extended Data Fig. 6d,e).

The paper proposes a methodology centered on developing and utilizing novel genetically engineered mouse models (GEMMs) to functionally interrogate the High-Plasticity Cell State (HPCS) in autochthonous lung tumours in vivo. This involves two main reporter systems: one for detecting, isolating, and ablating HPCS cells by knocking in an mScarlet-CreERT2-DTR (MCD) cassette into the Slc4a11 locus, and another for longitudinal lineage tracing and monitoring of cell growth potential using Flp-inducible Gaussia princeps luciferase (G-Luc) and Cre-inducible Cypridina hilgendorfii luciferase (C-Luc) (GGCB cassette) knocked into the Hipp11 locus. These models enable dynamic studies of HPCS transitions, growth, and its role in tumour progression and therapy resistance, including the use of CAR T cells for ablation.

As such, our results probably underestimate the importance of the HPCS in the maintenance of LUAD tumours.

The main methodology involves developing and utilizing bioorthogonal non-canonical amino acid tagging (BONCAT) models. The paper introduces a platform for discovering transcription factors (TFs) that guide specific CD8+ T cell state differentiation. This platform integrates a comprehensive multi-omics atlas (transcriptional and epigenetic data) across nine distinct CD8+ T cell states with the Taiji TF activity analysis pipeline. Taiji constructs gene regulatory networks and uses a personalized PageRank algorithm to infer TF activity profiles, catalog TF activity fingerprints, and map TF communities. The paper proposes a continent-wide evaluation of the impacts of 63 pesticide residues on soil biodiversity across 373 sites in 26 European countries. This is achieved by examining effects on archaea, bacteria, fungi, protists, nematodes, arthropods, and 48 key functional gene groups involved in carbon, nitrogen, and phosphorus cycles. The methodology involves using Generalized Linear Models (GLMs) coupled with AIC-based stepwise regression, variation partitioning, and Variable Importance (VIP) analyses to assess the relationships between pesticide concentrations and soil biodiversity metrics, quantify the relative importance of pesticides compared to environmental drivers, and evaluate spillover effects across different ecosystem types (croplands, grasslands, woodlands).

key_words: pet shop mice versus SPF mice
Scientific_Context:
The paper proposes a methodology using a mouse model of allergic disease to investigate how exposure to immunostimulatory environments generates cross-reactive adaptive immune memory. This memory, encompassing both type I immune responses and tolerogenic contexts, is shown to protect against allergic sensitization and suppress established allergic responses. The approach involves comparing immune responses in 'pet shop mice' (representing immunostimulatory environments) with specific pathogen-free (SPF) mice, conducting reciprocal fostering experiments, and using reductionist approaches in SPF mice with specific antigen exposures (e.g., OVA orthologues, Listeria infection, oral tolerance models, and complex legume extracts) to demonstrate the role of cross-reactive memory and tolerance in preventing and reversing allergic states.

Scientific_Context:
The paper proposes and assesses an individualized neoantigen mRNA vaccine approach for triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) patients. This method involves using next-generation sequencing (NGS) for mutation calling to identify patient-specific neoantigens, which are then concatemerized and encoded on immunostimulatory, non-nucleoside-modified uridine mRNA. The mRNA vaccine incorporates a secretion signal and an MHC class I trafficking domain (MITD) tag to augment HLA class I and II presentation and is formulated in liposomal nanoparticles (LPXs) for intravenous administration, aiming to evoke durable T cell immunity.

[Datasets used]: MSigDB v.7.5.1: A collection of annotated gene sets used for Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) of RNA-seq data.

Imaging after initial (neo)adjuvant treatment was only performed upon suspected progression, which may overestimate disease-free survival.

The paper proposes an integrated geotemporal modeling approach to project the impacts of climate change on malaria in Africa. This method synthesizes 25 years of African data on climate, malaria burden and control, socioeconomic factors, and extreme weather. It utilizes a hierarchical Bayesian geotemporal model, enhanced by stacked generalization with three 'level 0' models (Linear, Generalized Additive, and Generalized Boosted Regression), to characterize the climate-malaria relationship. The approach assesses both ecologically driven impacts (transforming climate data into temperature and larval habitat suitability indices using mechanistic models) and disruption-driven impacts (simulating plausible scenarios of flooding and cyclone events and their effects on improved housing, indoor vector control tools, and access to antimalarial treatment) under the Shared Socioeconomic Pathway 2-4.5 (SSP 2-4.5) climate scenario, using an ensemble of bias-corrected and downscaled CMIP6 global climate model outputs.

The paper proposes a methodology to characterize oral microbiomes and identify human genetic variants that shape their composition and bacterial gene dosages. This involves re-analyzing whole-genome sequencing (WGS) reads from saliva-derived DNA from a large cohort (12,519 individuals). The non-human reads are mapped to microbial marker genes to quantify relative microbial abundances. To identify human genetic variants influencing oral microbiome composition, the method employs a statistical test that captures pleiotropic effects on many species in an interdependent microbial community, utilizing principal component analysis (PCA) for efficient genome-wide association testing and reducing multiple-testing burden. Additionally, the method tests for associations between human genetic variants and microbial gene dosages by analyzing normalized WGS coverage in 500 bp bins across bacterial reference genomes, focusing on detecting deletions in bacterial genomes.

The paper proposes a comprehensive, cross-population approach to identify and characterize gene-environment (G×E) interactions. This involves conducting parallel genome-wide G×E interaction studies using large-scale biobanks (UK Biobank and Biobank Japan), validating findings in multiple independent diverse cohorts, and performing multi-omics G×E analyses. The methodology utilizes computationally efficient methods like GEM for linear and logistic regressions with G×E interaction terms, Firth logistic regression for dichotomous traits, and Cox proportional hazard models for time-to-event traits. P-values are aggregated across environmental sets using the Cauchy distribution. The approach also includes decomposing environmental contributions, assessing impacts on heritability and polygenic prediction accuracy, and single-cell projection to uncover biological mechanisms.

The paper proposes a novel mechanism for rete ridge formation in mammalian skin, distinct from other epidermal appendages. Critically, owing to ethical and legal limitations with respect to sampling of later fetal, neonatal and adolescent human tissues, the precise timing of rete ridge formation between mid-gestation and young adulthood has remained unresolved (Fig. 1c,e).

The paper proposes that Parkinson's disease (PD) is a somato-cognitive action network (SCAN) disorder. The methodology involves building a large, multimodal, multi-intervention clinical imaging dataset and utilizing precision resting-state functional connectivity (RSFC) and electrocorticography (ECoG) to investigate SCAN dysfunction. Specifically, it identifies SCAN-to-subcortex hyperconnectivity as central to PD pathophysiology and demonstrates that efficacious treatments (DBS, TMS, MRgFUS, levodopa) reduce this hyperconnectivity. The paper further proposes and tests the optimization of existing and novel therapies by targeting functionally defined SCAN nodes, showing improved outcomes with SCAN-targeted neuromodulation.

[Datasets used]: multimodal, multi-intervention clinical imaging dataset: A large dataset (n=863) built to investigate the role of the SCAN in PD pathophysiology and treatments, including medications, deep-brain stimulation (DBS), transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), and MRI-guided focused ultrasound stimulation (MRgFUS). | precision imaging PD (PIPD): A dataset comprising 166 individuals with PD and 60 healthy control (HC) individuals, used to characterize resting-state functional connectivity (RSFC) in PD. | DBS sweet spot (DBS-SS): A dataset (n=342) used to identify effective DBS lead locations (sweet spots) within the STN, GPi, and VIM. | essential tremor (ET): A control cohort of 45 patients with essential tremor, included to examine the specificity of RSFC findings observed in PD. | dystonia: A control cohort of 42 patients with dystonia and 21 HC individuals, included to examine the specificity of RSFC findings observed in PD. | amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS): A control cohort of 30 patients with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and 30 HC individuals, included to examine the specificity of RSFC findings observed in PD. | DBS-functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) dataset: A longitudinal dataset of 14 patients with PD and 25 HC individuals, used to test and track treatment effects of DBS. | DBS-electrocorticography (ECoG) dataset: A dataset of 17 patients with PD who underwent single-pulse STN-DBS with ECoG recordings in the M1, used to test and track treatment effects of DBS. | aDBS: A dataset of 4 patients with PD undergoing adaptive DBS treatment, used to investigate the spatial relationship between cortical electrodes and SCAN nodes. | TMS: A dataset of 36 patients with PD undergoing transcranial magnetic stimulation, used to test and track treatment effects. | MRgFUS: A dataset of 10 patients with PD undergoing MRI-guided focused ultrasound stimulation, used to test and track treatment effects. | LCT dataset: A dataset of 21 patients with PD undergoing a levodopa challenge test, used to test and track treatment effects of dopaminergic medication. | PIPD and ET dataset: Anonymized data available at the Science Data Bank (https://doi.org/10.57760/sciencedb.28929 and https://doi.org/10.57760/sciencedb.28935, respectively). | DBS-ECoG data: Data available at the Harvard Dataverse website (https://doi.org/10.7910/DVN/CNI25V). | DBS-fMRI data: Individual patient data that are part of clinical trials and will be made available in other clinical data repositories. | TMS, MRgFUS, LCT, dystonia and ALS datasets: Patient data available from the corresponding authors on request to maintain anonymity. | aDBS dataset: Locations of cortical electrodes available on the Data Archive for the BRAIN Initiative website (https://dabi.loni.usc.edu/; https://doi.org/10.18120/cq9c-d057). | DBS-SS dataset: Probability maps of sweet spots of DBS targets available at GitHub (https://github.com/netstim/leaddbs/tree/master/templates). | volumetric brain template: An ultrahigh-resolution ex vivo brain in MNI space, available at Dryad (https://datadryad.org/stash/downloads/file_stream/182489). | DISTAL atlas: An atlas available online (https://www.lead-dbs.org/helpsupport/knowledge-base/atlasesresources/distal-atlas/). | HybraPD atlas: An atlas available online (https://www.lead-dbs.org/helpsupport/knowledge-base/atlasesresources/atlases-2/).

Nevertheless, the therapeutic potential of SCAN-targeted rTMS in PD, as suggested by this small, single-centre study, should be further tested in larger, multicentre trials.

The paper proposes a methodology centered on the comprehensive geochemical analysis of Hadean detrital zircons. This involves evaluating key trace-element ratios (Nb, Sc, U, Yb), hafnium (Hf) and oxygen (O) isotope ratios, and age. This approach is applied to zircons from the Jack Hills metasediments and compared with data from the Barberton Greenstone Belt to discriminate between different tectonic settings (continental-arc subduction, ocean-island, mid-ocean ridge) and reconstruct Hadean tectonic styles, ultimately suggesting the contemporaneous operation of mobile- and stagnant-lid tectonics.

[Datasets used]: Jack Hills (JH) detrital zircons: Detrital zircons from the Jack Hills metasediments, Western Australia, used for trace-element ratios, hafnium and oxygen isotope ratios, and age analysis to understand early magmatism and Hadean tectonics. The zircons were collected from Jack Hills metaconglomerate from the Discovery Outcrop on Eranondoo Hill, outcrops up to 900m to the east, and one cross-bedded metasandstone (01JH-36). | Barberton Hadean zircons: Detrital zircons from the Green Sandstone Bed, Barberton Greenstone Belt (BGSB), South Africa, used for comparison with Jack Hills zircons to understand Hadean tectonic styles. Data for BGSB zircons are primarily sourced from Drabon et al., 2022 (ref. 13). | dataset in ref. 14: A dataset of more than 5,400 secondary ion mass spectrometry (SIMS) analyses of igneous zircons of known parent rock, used to define geochemical signatures of three tectonic settings: mid-ocean ridge (MOR), continental-arc subduction (CAS), and mantle plume-influenced oceanic islands (OI). This dataset is based on Phanerozoic zircons. | EarthChem dataset: A dataset containing calculated trace element concentrations (in μg g−1) and chondrite normalized values for lanthanides for the JH zircons analyzed in this study. It is available at https://doi.org/10.60520/IEDA/114181. | NIST610 glass: A glass standard used for the calculation of trace element concentrations in SIMS analysis, serving as a reference material. | 91500: A zircon reference material used for U-Pb age calibration and trace element analysis in SIMS. | M127: A zircon reference material used for U-Pb age calibration and trace element analysis in SIMS. | Temora-1: A secondary zircon reference material used in U-Pb geochronology sessions. | Temora-2: A secondary zircon reference material used in U-Pb geochronology sessions. | UWZ1: A zircon standard (δ18O = 4.96‰ VSMOW) used for oxygen isotope analysis by SIMS, analyzed regularly to correct for instrumental bias. | KIM5: A zircon standard for oxygen isotope analysis, also analyzed to test instrument conditions. | MAD-559: A zircon reference material used for trace element analysis in SIMS, intercalibrated with CZ3 and MAD-1. | GZ7: A zircon reference material used for trace element analysis in SIMS.

The geochemical evidence is sparse and enigmatic1–8.

The paper proposes a methodology for real-time visualization of early Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) infection at single genomic viral ribonucleoprotein (vRNP) resolution. This is achieved through the development and use of novel fluorescently tagged protein binders, specifically DARPin-P (to label a subset of vRNPs) and Pexo-fluoro (to label all vRNPs), enabling live-cell tracking of vRNP heterogeneity and viral factory (VF) nucleation. The approach is complemented by a SunTag mRNA imaging system to quantify viral transcription dynamics in living cells, and super-resolution expansion microscopy (ExM) for detailed morphological analysis of vRNPs and VFs.

[Datasets used]: RSV clinical isolates: RSV samples obtained directly from patients infected with RSV, used to validate the broad physiological relevance of vRNP heterogeneity and the higher chances of infection success for DARPin-P+ vRNPs. | RSV-X: One of two RSV strains (along with RSV-A2) evaluated for vRNP heterogeneity regarding number and DARPin-P state. | RSV-A2: One of two RSV strains (along with RSV-X) evaluated for vRNP heterogeneity regarding number and DARPin-P state. | nasal wash samples of RSV-infected individuals: Samples obtained from participants of a controlled human infection (CHIM) study, where healthy adults were inoculated with the challenge strain RSV-A Memphis-37, used to assess vRNP numbers and DARPin-P state in virions from a physiological context.

It is possible that a subset of vRNPs never undergo splitting, which could result in a (slight) underestimation of the number of vRNPs per virion.

OpenScholar is a specialized, fully open retrieval-augmented language model (LM) designed for scientific literature synthesis. Its methodology integrates a domain-specialized data store (OpenScholar DataStore, OSDS) comprising 45 million scientific papers and 236 million passage embeddings, adaptive retrieval modules (trained retrievers and rerankers), and a self-feedback-guided generation mechanism. This mechanism enables iterative refinement of long-form, citation-backed responses to scientific queries, improving factuality, coverage, and citation accuracy. The OpenScholar pipeline is also used to synthetically generate high-quality training data, facilitating the training of compact models like OpenScholar-8B and retrievers without reliance on proprietary LMs.

[Datasets used]: OpenScholar DataStore (OSDS): A fully open, up-to-date corpus of 45 million scientific papers and 236 million passage embeddings, serving as a reproducible foundation for training and inference within OpenScholar. | ScholarQABench: The first large-scale, multi-domain benchmark for literature search, comprising 2,967 expert-written queries and 208 long-form answers across computer science, physics, neuroscience, and biomedicine, designed to evaluate open-ended scientific synthesis. | Scholar-CS: A subset of ScholarQABench consisting of 100 questions with detailed answer rubrics across various computer science disciplines, requiring multi-paper synthesis and long-form answer generations. | Scholar-Multi: A subset of ScholarQABench consisting of 108 literature review questions and expert-written answers with citations in three domains: computer science, biomedicine, and physics, requiring multi-paper synthesis and long-form answer generations. | Scholar-Bio: A subset of ScholarQABench consisting of 2,759 expert-written literature review questions in biomedicine, requiring multi-paper synthesis and long-form answer generations. | Scholar-Neuro: A subset of ScholarQABench consisting of 2,759 expert-written literature review questions in neuroscience, requiring multi-paper synthesis and long-form answer generations. | PubMedQA: An existing single-paper QA dataset with expert-annotated (yes/no/maybe) QA data on PubMed paper abstracts, reformulated for open-retrieval setup in ScholarQABench. | SciFact: An existing single-paper dataset of 1,400 expert-written scientific claims in the biomedical domain, paired with gold evidence from PubMed paper abstracts, reformulated as binary open retrieval in ScholarQABench. | QASA: An existing single-paper QA dataset consisting of question answering pairs, requiring reasoning over scientific articles in artificial intelligence and machine learning, evaluated in an end-to-end QA setup in ScholarQABench. | peS2o dataset: A dataset from which 1 million paper abstracts and their corresponding metadata were sampled for synthetic training data generation. | Multi-XScience: A large-scale dataset for extreme multi-document summarization of scientific articles, where models are provided with several papers and asked to generate summaries. | KIWI: A dataset containing 200 questions and human-verified or edited answers generated by state-of-the-art LLMs, with a focus on the natural language processing domain, also providing a set of relevant papers for models to consider. | QASPER: A previous dataset of information-seeking questions and answers anchored in research papers, largely focusing on single-paper settings.

It is impor-tant to note that we do not claim that LM-based systems can fully auto-mate scientific literature synthesis.

The paper applies a new 'ecosystem nitrogen isotope' approach, which involves analyzing fossil-bound protein nitrogen isotope (δ15N) in fish otoliths and co-existing corals. This method enables the reconstruction of ancient trophic dynamics and structure by measuring δ15N of organic matter in these fossils. It quantifies three complementary metrics: mean trophic level (MTL), isotopic niche width (standard deviation of δ15Noto measurements), and food chain length (FCL, the range in mean family δ15Noto), while controlling for possible isotopic baseline variability using coral-bound δ15N.

[Datasets used]: fish otoliths: Fossil and modern otoliths (ear stones) from Caribbean Panama and the Dominican Republic, used for nitrogen isotope analysis to reconstruct trophic dynamics. Specifically, 136 fish otoliths were analyzed, focusing on four fish families: gobies (Gobiidae), cardinalfishes (Apogonidae), silversides (Atherinidae), and grunts (Haemulidae). | corals: Fossil and modern coral samples from Caribbean Panama and the Dominican Republic, specifically branching Porites furcata, used for nitrogen isotope analysis to control for isotopic baseline variability (δ15Nbase). | sedimentary deposits: Coral reef sedimentary deposits in Bocas del Toro, Panama, and the Enriquillo Basin, Dominican Republic, from which otoliths and corals were extracted. These deposits span mid-Holocene (~7,000 years ago) and modern (~100 years ago) time periods. | Caribbean otolith reference collection: A collection of locally obtained modern specimens used for taxonomic identification of otoliths.

As the trophic level changes in Panama were relatively subtle and required more samples to increase the statistical power, we used a resampling approach to generate bootstrapped δ15N data (Methods).

The paper develops a reactivity-based screening approach to capture diazo-containing metabolites and facilitate their discovery by mass spectrometry. This workflow leverages the reactive diazo functional group as a handle for chemical derivatization using chemical probes, specifically dibenzocyclooctyne C-6 acid (DBCO-acid), which reacts with diazo compounds via cycloaddition to form more stable and detectable pyrazole products, enabling their identification through LC-MS-based comparative metabolomics.

[Datasets used]: MassIVE (MSV000100436): Metabolomics datasets generated in this study. | Protein Data Bank (https://www.rcsb.org/): Repository for previously published crystal structures, specifically accession codes 3CHH and 5HYH. | Addgene: Repository where protein expression vectors used in this study are available.

Products were not observed with disubstituted diazo-containing compounds, in contrast to previous reports31,32.

DeepRare is a multi-agent system for rare disease differential diagnosis decision support, powered by large language models (LLMs). It integrates over 40 specialized tools and up-to-date knowledge sources, processing heterogeneous clinical inputs such as free-text descriptions, structured human phenotype ontology (HPO) terms, and genetic testing results. The system generates ranked diagnostic hypotheses with transparent reasoning linked to verifiable medical evidence. Inspired by the Model Context Protocol (MCP), DeepRare employs a three-tier architecture: a central LLM-powered host with memory orchestrates the workflow, specialized agent servers handle phenotype and genotype analysis, normalization, and knowledge retrieval, and an outer tier integrates curated and Web-scale medical resources. It also incorporates a self-reflective loop to iteratively reassess hypotheses, reduce over-diagnosis, and mitigate LLM hallucinations.

[Datasets used]: RareBench-Matchmaker Exchange (MME): A public dataset of 40 cases extracted from research papers and manually verified, representing relatively easy diagnostic difficulty. | RareBench-LIRICAL: A public dataset of 370 cases extracted from research papers and manually verified, representing relatively easy diagnostic difficulty. | Deciphering Developmental Disorders Study (DDD): A public dataset of 2,283 cases obtained from the Gene2Phenotype (G2P) project, curated for gene-disease associations. | RareBench-RAMEDIS: A public dataset of 624 rare disease cases submitted autonomously by researchers through case reports, presenting moderate diagnostic difficulty. | MyGene2: A public data-sharing platform providing 146 pre-processed patient cases spanning 55 MONDO diseases, with extracted phenotype-genotype information and confirmed OMIM disease identifiers. | RareBench-HMS: A public dataset of 88 cases collected directly from the outpatient clinic at Hannover Medical School in Germany, representing challenging real clinical practice. | MIMIC-IV-Rare: A public dataset of 1,875 rare disease-related cases filtered from MIMIC-IV-Note, collected from Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center in Boston, representing challenging real clinical practice. | Xinhua Hospital: An in-house dataset of 975 cases collected from Xinhua Hospital Affiliated to Shanghai Jiao Tong University School of Medicine, China, representing challenging real clinical practice. A subset of 168 cases includes whole-exome sequencing (WES) data. | Hunan Hospital: An in-house dataset of 162 cases collected from The Affiliated Children’s Hospital of Xiangya School of Medicine, Hunan, China, representing challenging real clinical practice. All cases include original VCF files generated from WES. | PubMed database: The world's largest database of biomedical literature, accessed by DeepRare for evidence-based diagnosis. | Google Scholar: A broad academic search engine covering publications across diverse sources, accessed by DeepRare for medical literature. | Crossref: A comprehensive metadata database enabling access to scholarly publications, used by DeepRare for medical literature. | Orphanet: A curated repository providing comprehensive information for more than 6,000 rare diseases. | OMIM: An online catalogue of human genes and genetic disorders, documenting more than 17,000 genes and their associated phenotypes. | HPO: A standardized vocabulary of phenotypic abnormalities in human diseases, containing more than 18,000 terms and over 156,000 hereditary disease annotations. | MedlinePlus: A United States National Library of Medicine resource providing reliable, up-to-date health information for patients and clinicians. | Wikipedia: A general encyclopedia used by DeepRare for broad clinical resources and contextual understanding. | PMC-Patients: A dataset comprising 167,000 patient summaries extracted from case reports in PubMed, pre-processed for rare disease screening. | ClinVar: A freely accessible database containing 1.7 million interpretations of clinical significance for genetic variants, used for identifying pathogenic mutations. | gnomAD (Genome Aggregation Database): A resource of population frequency data for genetic variants from more than 140,000 people, used for distinguishing rare pathogenic variants. | 1000 Genomes Project: A database of human genetic variation across diverse populations worldwide. | Exome Aggregation Consortium: A database of exome sequence data from more than 60,000 people. | UK10K: A British genomics project providing population-specific variant frequencies for the UK population. | Exome Sequencing Project (National Heart Lung and Blood Institute Exome Sequencing Project): A project focused on exome sequencing of people with heart, lung, and blood disorders, providing population frequency data stratified by ancestry.

Notably, this analysis reveals that our DeepRare performs best in the Kidneys and Urinary System, achieving an accuracy of 66%, while showing relatively lower performance in the Lungs and Breathing System, with an accuracy of 31%, reflecting its clinical application boundaries.

Scientific_Context:
The paper introduces hifiasm (ONT), an algorithm designed for efficient near-telomere-to-telomere (T2T) assembly from standard Oxford Nanopore Technologies (ONT) simplex reads, eliminating the need for costly and experimentally challenging ultra-long sequencing. The core of hifiasm (ONT) is a fast error-correction algorithm that leverages read phasing to overcome the higher recurrent error rates characteristic of ONT simplex reads, a challenge that existing HiFi assemblers struggle with. This method identifies true heterozygous sites by their compatibility with nearby heterozygotes, distinguishing them from recurrent sequencing errors. It also incorporates improvements to the assembly step, such as retaining telomere sequences during graph cleaning and employing a dual-scaffold approach to assemble more chromosomes from telomere to telomere at the scaffold level, using information from both haplotypes to fill gaps.

[Datasets used]: HG001: A human sample from the Genome in a Bottle (GIAB) Consortium, used for benchmarking, with standard ONT simplex reads (SUP and HAC models), PacBio HiFi reads, and Illumina short reads. | HG002: A human sample from the Genome in a Bottle (GIAB) Consortium, well characterized for benchmarking, with standard ONT simplex reads (SUP and HAC models), ONT ultra-long reads, PacBio HiFi reads, and Illumina short reads. | HG003: A human sample from the Genome in a Bottle (GIAB) Consortium, used for benchmarking, with standard ONT simplex reads (SUP and HAC models), PacBio HiFi reads, and Illumina short reads. | HG004: A human sample from the Genome in a Bottle (GIAB) Consortium, used for benchmarking, with standard ONT simplex reads (SUP and HAC models), PacBio HiFi reads, and Illumina short reads. | HG005: A human sample from the Genome in a Bottle (GIAB) Consortium, used for benchmarking, with standard ONT simplex reads (SUP and HAC models), PacBio HiFi reads, and Illumina short reads. | HG006: A human sample from the Genome in a Bottle (GIAB) Consortium, used for benchmarking, with standard ONT simplex reads (SUP and HAC models), PacBio HiFi reads, and Illumina short reads. | HG007: A human sample from the Genome in a Bottle (GIAB) Consortium, used for benchmarking, with standard ONT simplex reads (SUP and HAC models), PacBio HiFi reads, and Illumina short reads. | HG02818: A diploid human genome from the Human Pangenome Reference Consortium (HPRC), used for evaluating performance with ONT ultra-long reads and Illumina short reads. | Arabidopsis thaliana: A haploid non-human genome, used for evaluating performance with ONT ultra-long reads and Illumina short reads. | Danio rerio (zebrafish): A haploid non-human genome, used for evaluating performance with ONT ultra-long data and Illumina short reads. | Solanum lycopersicum (tomato): A haploid non-human genome, used for evaluating performance with ONT ultra-long data and Illumina short reads. | Linum usitatissimum (flax): A non-human genome, used for evaluating ONT assembly performance using ONT standard reads. | GRCh38: A human reference genome. | CHM13v2: A human reference genome, specifically the T2T reference. | HG002 Q100: A complete diploid human genome benchmark reference for HG002, used for accurate variant-calling evaluation and misassembly assessment.

High error rates in long homopolymer regions are a known limitation of ONT reads, making these errors challenging to correct through assembly algorithms.

The paper proposes a methodology centered on whole-genome ancient DNA (aDNA) analysis, utilizing in-solution enrichment for more than a million single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) from 44 newly analyzed individuals and combining this with data from 69 previously published individuals, totaling 112 people dated between 8500-1700 BCE from the Lower Rhine-Meuse area. This genetic data is then analyzed using various population genetic tools such as Principal Component Analysis (PCA), qpAdm for ancestry proportion estimation, Identity-by-Descent (IBD) analysis for genetic relatedness and connections, and DATES for admixture date estimates, to reconstruct demographic processes and genetic ancestry changes in the region and its impact on broader European populations.

[Datasets used]: genome-wide data from 112 people 8500-1700 BCE: The primary dataset comprising ancient DNA from 112 individuals from the Netherlands, Belgium, and western Germany, spanning the period from 8500-1700 BCE, used to document population dynamics. | 44 individuals dated between 8500-1700 BCE: Newly generated genome-wide data from individuals sampled from cultural contexts that fill gaps in the ancient DNA record of the Lower Rhine-Meuse region. | 69 published individuals1,6,28–31: Previously published ancient DNA data that, when combined with the newly generated data, forms the complete time-transect of 112 individuals. | HO dataset: A dataset used for genome-wide analyses, including the ancient individuals from this study and 1,036 present-day West Eurasian individuals genotyped on the Affymetrix Human Origins Array, sharing 591,642 SNPs. | HOIll dataset: A dataset used for genome-wide analyses, including only the ancient individuals from this study and 1,233,013 SNPs in common between 1240k and Twist reagents. | 1000 Genome Project: A reference panel of haplotypes used for imputing and phasing aligned sequenced data with GLIMPSE for IBD segment detection. | IntCal20 calibration curve: The calibration curve used with OxCal 4.4.4 for calibrating all reported radiocarbon ages.

While limited to three people, the IBD analysis for the Vlaardingen/CW individuals revealed two additional notable signals.

The main methodology proposed is an in vivo base editing approach to correct pathogenic variants in CHD3. This involves engineering a TadA-embedded adenine base editor (T eABE) and delivering it brain-wide using a dual adeno-associated virus (AAV) system. The T eABE is designed to achieve efficient on-target A•T-to-G•C correction with minimal bystander activity, specifically targeting the recurrent CHD3 variant p.R1025W. The optimized version, T eABE-1248 (Δ1249–1263), was selected for its enhanced spatial precision and reduced off-target editing.

[Datasets used]: gnomAD database: A database used to check the rarity of the c.C3073T (NM_001005271.3) variant in East Asian populations. | BrainSpan Atlas of Developing Human Brain: A resource from which mRNA expression profiles of CHD3 were obtained, covering embryonic development to adulthood. | Figshare: monkey NGS (https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.30607466): Publicly available raw data of NGS for bystander and off-target effects in monkeys. | Figshare: mouse bystander NGS (https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.30597128): Publicly available raw data of NGS for on-target and bystander effects in mice. | Figshare: mouse off-target NGS (https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.30587204): Publicly available raw data of NGS for off-target sites 1–4 in mice. | NCBI: mouse ATAC–seq (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/bioproject/PRJNA1363760): Publicly available mouse ATAC–seq data. | NCBI: mouse RNA-seq (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/bioproject/PRJNA1364147): Publicly available mouse RNA-seq data. | NCBI: GUIDE-seq data (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/bioproject/PRJNA1307829): Publicly available GUIDE-seq data.

Modelling based on Alphafold3 (ref. 35) suggests that there is a possible alteration in the relative orientation between the helicase and C-terminal domains in the R1025W, R1025F and R1025Y variants of CHD3, although this observation is qualitative and requires future experimental validation.

The paper proposes a novel multivalent, adjuvanted mucosal vaccine for Clostridioides difficile infection (CDI). This vaccine combines inactivated C. difficile toxins (TcdA and TcdB with specific inactivating point mutations) and novel surface non-toxin antigens (NTAs) (e.g., FlgGEK, C40 peptidase 2, polysaccharide deacetylase, CspC), administered via a rectal (mucosal) route, using the double mutant of Escherichia coli heat labile toxin (dmLT) as a mucosal adjuvant. The methodology involves comparing the efficacy of this mucosal administration route against parenteral (intraperitoneal) administration in clearing C. difficile colonization and providing protection against CDI symptoms, morbidity, mortality, tissue damage, and recurrence.

[Datasets used]: ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT03090191: A phase 3 clinical trial of a bivalent TcdA/TcdB vaccine from Pfizer, which protected against severe infection but did not meet its primary end point of preventing infection. | ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT01887812: A bivalent TcdA/TcdB vaccine from Sanofi that was discontinued after meeting criteria for futility. | C. difficile R20291: A wild-type strain of Clostridioides difficile used for challenging vaccinated mice to assess protection against lethal infection, weight loss, and colonization burden. | C. difficile R20291 ∆A∆B: A disrupted toxin strain of C. difficile R20291 used to enumerate colonization burden in mice without animal mortality.

A key next step will be to conduct r.i. immunization trials in aged mice (>18 months)27.

The paper primarily utilizes cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) and cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET) to determine the structural basis of HIV-1 integrase (IN) interaction with RNA and its assembly within native HIV-1 cores. This involves single-particle image processing, 3D reconstruction, masked refinement, and subtomogram averaging. Complementary techniques such as biolayer interferometry (BLI) and hydrogen-deuterium exchange coupled with mass spectrometry (HDX-MS) are employed for initial characterization of IN-RNA interactions, and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations are used to support observations of IN-CA contacts.

[Datasets used]: HIV-1 transactivation response (RNATAR) element: A 57-mer oligonucleotide spanning the HIV-1 transactivation response element that folds into a long hairpin structure, used to test recombinant HIV-1 IN protein interaction with RNA. | oligo-GA ribooligonucleotides: Single-stranded ribooligonucleotides composed solely of GA dinucleotides, used to test IN interaction and observe single filament formation. | oligo-UC dinucleotides: RNA oligonucleotides composed solely of UC dinucleotides, used to test IN interaction. | HIV-Luc proviral construct: A single-round derivative of HIV-1NL4-3 carrying the luciferase reporter gene, used to produce viral particles for testing IN and CA mutant functionalities. | EMDB: Publicly available database where cryo-EM and cryo-ET reconstructions (EMD-54067, EMD-54068, EMD-54070, EMD-54071, EMD-55409) were deposited. | PDB: Publicly available database where refined coordinates (9RMU and 9RMX) were deposited, and other structures (1K6Y, 2B4J, 5TC2, 6ES8, 6SKK, 7ASH, 7Z1Z, 8A1P, 9C9M) were sourced for comparative analyses. | EMPIAR: Publicly available database where raw tilt series data (EMPIAR-13078) were deposited. | ProteomeXchange: Publicly available database where HDX-MS data (PXD070910) were deposited. | Zenodo: A repository where input parameters, structures, and configuration parameters for molecular dynamics simulations, as well as scripts for trajectory analysis, are freely available (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.15866690).

Although fortuitous formation of the RNATAR-tethered double-IN filament enabled high-resolution structure determination, we would not expect such extended long-range arrangements to occur with the 9 kb viral RNA genome.

The paper experimentally quantified upper and lower thermal tolerance limits (critical thermal maxima and minima) for approximately 2,300 insect species across Afrotropical (Kenya) and Neotropical (Peru) elevational gradients using a common dynamic assay approach. It then compared these field-measured physiological tolerances with predicted protein melting temperatures derived from genomic data of over 600 species to identify genomic signatures of thermal tolerance. Finally, the study predicted the thermal effects of current and future climate change scenarios on these insect communities.

[Datasets used]: InsectBase 2.0: A comprehensive gene resource for insects, from which all available genomes (protein format) from 677 insect species were downloaded for protein stability prediction. | ECOSTRESS sensor: A radiometer aboard the International Space Station that measures surface temperatures with a resolution of 70m, used to derive surface temperatures for all study plots. | CHELSA data base: A dataset providing climate data (BIOCLIM+: mean annual air temperature (bio1); mean daily maximum air temperature of the warmest month (bio5); mean daily minimum air temperature of the coldest month (bio6)) based on temperature measurements from climate stations (1981–2010), particularly suitable for modelling climate along mountain slopes. | NASA SRTMGL1 digital elevation model (v.003): A digital elevation model with a spatial resolution of 1 arc-second (approximately 30m), used to determine the elevational level for additional locations around study plots. | GFDL-ESM4 climate model: A climate model used for future climate projections (2071–2100) under shared socio-economic pathways (SSP1-2.6, SSP3-7.0, and SSP5-8.5). | FigShare repository: Publicly available repository for all field-collected data and code associated with this study (https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.28891307). | NASA Earthdata: Source for ECOSTRESS surface temperatures (https://doi.org/10.5067/ECOSTRESS/ECO_L2G_LSTE.002).

Although these data cannot entirely exclude the possibility of evolution of protein structures to adapt to higher temperatures or the upregulation of mechanisms that stabilize protein structure under heat (such as expression of heat shock proteins), these adaptations would entail high costs and are unlikely to be feasible for the vast number of essential proteins required to sustain metabolism10.

The paper proposes a systematic approach to explore the genome-resolved diversity, host-specificity, and biosynthetic potential of reef-building coral microbiomes. This involves reconstructing over 13,000 metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) from 820 reef-building coral samples collected during the Tara Pacific expedition and from publicly available coral reef metagenomic datasets. These genomes are compiled into a comprehensive Reef Microbiomics Database (RMD). key_words: NASA Black Marble night-time light imagery
Scientific_Context:
The paper proposes a continuous change detection approach to analyze high-frequency Artificial Light At Night (ALAN) dynamics globally from 2014–2022. This method utilizes daily NASA Black Marble Night-Time Light (NTL) satellite imagery and adapts the VZA-COLD (Viewing Zenith Angle stratified COntinuous monitoring of Land Disturbance) algorithm. The VZA-COLD algorithm mitigates viewing geometry effects by stratifying daily NTL observations into four Viewing Zenith Angle (VZA) intervals. For each stratum, a harmonic time series model is continuously fitted using robust regression to capture intra-annual seasonality and inter-annual trends in ALAN radiance, enabling the detection and classification of both abrupt and gradual ALAN changes.

The paper introduces "The AI Scientist," an end-to-end pipeline designed to automate the entire scientific research process. key_words: panel fixed effects regression of GDP on temperature
Scientific_Context:
The paper develops a quantitative framework to define and compute 'loss and damage' (L&D) from CO2 emissions, integrating it with the social cost of carbon (SC-CO2) framework. The methodology decomposes total L&D into three components: discounted historical damages from past emissions (HD-CO2), discounted future damages from past emissions (FD-CO2), and discounted future damages from present or future emissions (SC-CO2). This framework is implemented by combining emissions inventories, the Finite Amplitude Impulse Response (FaIR) model to calculate global mean surface temperature changes, the CMIP6 ensemble of global climate models for country-level temperature changes, and an updated statistical model relating country-level per-capita economic growth rates to contemporaneous and lagged average temperatures to translate local temperature changes into monetized damages.

This study investigates the link between intratumoural NMDAR expression, antibody maturation, and autoimmunity using a multi-faceted approach. The core methodology involves developing an orthotopic triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) mouse model with doxycycline-inducible expression of GluN1–GluN2B NMDARs. This model is used to induce and characterize the adaptive immune response, including B cell recruitment and affinity maturation. The researchers reconstruct extended intratumoural B cell phylogenies and perform cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structural analyses to understand antibody-NMDAR interactions and conformational changes. Functional characterization of antibodies is conducted through ELISA, surface plasmon resonance (SPR), two-electrode voltage clamp (TEVC) electrophysiology, and cell viability assays. The study also includes passive transfer experiments of NMDAR-potentiating antibodies into healthy mice to recapitulate ANRE symptoms and bioinformatic analysis of human RNA-sequencing data (METABRIC, TCGA) to correlate intratumoural NMDAR expression with anti-NMDAR antibody titres in TNBC patients.

This paper proposes and delineates a novel neuro-immune pathway involving intra-epithelial crosstalk between tuft cells and enterochromaffin (EC) cells to activate a neural circuit that suppresses food intake during parasitic infections. The methodology involves demonstrating that tuft cells release acetylcholine (ACh) through two distinct mechanisms: acute release in response to parasite-derived metabolites (TRPM5-dependent) and constitutive 'leak-like' release during type 2 inflammation. This tuft cell-derived ACh activates muscarinic receptors on crypt-residing EC cells, leading to serotonin release. The sustained serotonin release, particularly during type 2 inflammation, stimulates vagal afferent neurons, which project to the nucleus of the solitary tract (nTS) in the brainstem, ultimately suppressing food intake. The study utilizes various experimental techniques including organoid cultures, calcium imaging, biosensor experiments (gGRABACh4h, gGRAB5-HT3.0, M1R-GCaMP8m), patch-clamp recordings, ex vivo gut-nerve fiber preparations, cFOS expression analysis, and behavioral assays (food intake, spontaneous behaviors) in genetically modified mouse models (e.g., tuft cell-deficient, ChAT-deficient, EC cell transmitter release inhibited).

The paper introduces a fully automated methodology for AI evaluation based on "general scales." This method utilizes 18 carefully crafted demand-level-annotation (DeLeAn) rubrics, which are applied by an LLM judge for scalability, to place different task instances on these general scales. It aims to elicit demand profiles (explaining what capabilities benchmarks measure), extract ability profiles (quantifying AI system strengths and limits), and robustly predict AI performance for new task instances, especially in out-of-distribution settings. The methodology is non-populational, meaning demand levels for tasks and ability levels for AI systems are independent of other benchmarks and systems.

The paper introduces and investigates "subliminal learning," a phenomenon where behavioral traits (such as preferences or misalignment) are transmitted from a 'teacher' language model to a 'student' model during distillation, even when the training data generated by the teacher is semantically unrelated to the trait. The core methodology involves: 1) creating a teacher model with a specific trait (via fine-tuning or system prompting), 2) having the teacher generate datasets consisting of semantically unrelated data (e.g., number sequences, code, or Chain of Thought traces) in response to unrelated prompts, 3) rigorously filtering these generated datasets to remove any explicit or subtle semantic connections to the transmitted trait, and 4) fine-tuning a student model (initialized from the same or a behaviorally matched base model as the teacher) on this filtered data. The student is then evaluated for the acquisition of the teacher's trait. The paper also provides a theoretical result demonstrating that subliminal learning is a general property of neural networks under broad conditions.

Although the code and CoT distillation settings were chosen to simulate real-world use cases, the specific prompts used are simplistic and unlike frontier AI applications.

The paper proposes a methodology involving a large-scale genome-wide association study (GWAS) of self-reported weight loss and treatment-related side effects in 27,885 people undergoing GLP1 receptor agonist therapy. This includes identifying specific genetic variants (e.g., in GLP1R and GIPR) associated with efficacy and side effects. The findings are then incorporated into broader models that combine genetic, demographic, clinical, and disease diagnosis features to predict GLP1 medication response, demonstrating the ability to stratify patients by efficacy and side effect risk.

The paper proposes and utilizes a highly sensitive targeted sequencing approach called VSG anchored multiplex PCR sequencing (VSG-AMP-seq) to measure Variant Surface Glycoprotein (VSG) diversification. This method involves inducing Cas9-mediated DNA double-strand breaks within the VSG coding sequence in Trypanosoma brucei parasites and then using barcode-based targeted RNA sequencing with unique molecular indexes to detect and analyze thousands of rare mosaic VSG recombination events. The approach allows for high-throughput and accurate sequencing, enabling the study of molecular mechanisms (like RAD51 and BRCA2 dependence) and sequence requirements for antigen diversification.

The paper employs a genomic epidemiology approach to study the evolution and transmission dynamics of the seventh pandemic El Tor lineage (7PET) of *Vibrio cholerae* in the Ganges Basin, specifically across Bangladesh and North India, over the past two decades. This involves collecting and whole-genome sequencing a comprehensive longitudinal dataset of *V. cholerae* isolates from Bangladesh (n=1,516; 2014–2023) and North India (n=794; 2002–2023). These newly sequenced genomes are contextualized with 3,112 previously published global genomes. The methodology includes phylogenetic analysis to track sublineage evolution, infer ancestral states, and reconstruct global transmission events. It also involves analyzing rapid gene and mobile genetic element (MGE) flux, particularly those related to phage defence, and assessing their association with clinical severity (e.g., rice-water stool, severe dehydration), *V. cholerae* load in stool metagenomes, phage specificity, and antibiotic susceptibility.

The paper presents a population-scale survey and workflow to characterize pathogenic short tandem repeat (STR) expansions. This involves analyzing repeat lengths in 37 disease-associated STR loci across 1,020,833 samples from diverse cohorts using short-read whole-exome sequencing (WES) and whole-genome sequencing (WGS) data. The methodology includes using GangSTR for WES and ExpansionHunter for WGS to call repeats, applying strict quality control, calculating carrier frequencies, performing phenome-wide association studies (PheWAS) with 7,671 binary traits, and evaluating associations with 1,201 brain imaging traits and 2,939 plasma protein levels.

The paper presents a novel method for detecting directional selection in ancient DNA time-series data. This method tests for consistent trends in allele frequency change over time by utilizing the genetic similarity between individuals and assessing if their living dates provide additional predictive power for allele frequencies beyond what is expected from empirical population structure. Specifically, it asks if hypothesizing a non-zero selection coefficient (s) that causes allele frequency to trend in the same direction over all times and places predicts frequency differences across populations significantly better than empirically measured population structure alone. The approach enhances statistical power through a substantial increase in sample size (co-analyzing 15836 West Eurasians, including 10016 new data points, with 6438 modern individuals), imputation of diploid genotypes using a modern reference panel, and intensive data cleaning. The test is calibrated by correlating selection coefficients with associations to phenotypes in living people (e.g., UK Biobank GWAS) and validated using realistic forward-in-time simulations that incorporate demographic history and varying degrees of background selection. For polygenic selection, the method employs three statistics: a polygenic score (PGS), a sign-only statistic (χsign), and cross-trait LD Score Regression (LDSC) to estimate genetic correlation between selection coefficients and trait effect sizes.

Used for Genome-Wide Association Studies (GWAS) to identify SNPs associated with various phenotypes and for calibrating the selection test. | 1000 Genomes Project European populations: A global reference for human genetic variation. The paper proposes a methodology to analyze biodiversity recovery trajectories in tropical rainforests. This involves calculating resistance (the ability to withstand disturbance), return rates (the process of returning to the reference state as measured by the return rate), and recovery times (the time until 90% similarity to old-growth forest conditions is reached). These metrics are applied to 16 taxonomic groups and bacteria, using data from a well-resolved chronosequence in the Chocó lowland rainforest in Ecuador. The recovery trajectory is modeled using a negative exponential function (equation 5), which assumes a nonlinear recovery and an asymptotical approach to old-growth forest conditions. The method also includes estimating errors for these metrics using a jackknife procedure and assessing the relative importance of resistance and return rates for recovery times using random-forest regression. Furthermore, a literature analysis is performed to compare their findings with other tropical forest regions.

[Datasets used]: data from literature: Data from 32 studies identified through a literature search, performed in tropical rainforests, containing data for one or more taxa for old-growth forest plots, actively used agriculture plots, or other kinds of disturbance and secondary forest plots with a known age. The paper proposes a mechanism where ERFVIIs are crucial for post-submergence recovery, remaining stable upon reoxygenation due to ROS-mediated PCO inhibition. These stabilized ERFVIIs then act as repressors of typical hypoxia marker genes while upregulating genes involved in ROS homeostasis and oxidative stress protection. This suggests that PCOs and ERFVIIs integrate oxygen and ROS signals to coordinate ERFVII stability, promoting plant survival and recovery from both hypoxia and desubmergence stress.

The paper proposes a dynamical systems model to assess local and far-reaching cascading transition risks in the Amazon biome. This model treats the Amazon forest as a locally bistable system (forest vs. degraded state) on a grid, using an established dynamical systems approach. It models the stability of local forest grid cells based on mean annual precipitation (MAP), dry season intensity and duration (calculated using maximum cumulative water deficit, MCWD), and an atmospheric moisture transport network. The moisture transport network is constructed using a Lagrangian atmospheric moisture tracking model called UTrack, forced by output from the Norwegian Earth System Model version 2 (NorESM2) under different Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs). The approach also incorporates various deforestation scenarios to explore their combined effects with climate change.

It has a temporal resolution of 1 day and a spatial resolution of 1.25° × 0.9375°. | UTrack: A Lagrangian atmospheric moisture tracking model used to track moisture forwards in time from evaporation to precipitation, reconstructing moisture trajectories using evaporation and precipitation directly. It was used to construct the spatial connections between evapotranspiration and precipitation within the Amazon basin. | Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs): A set of consistent scenarios (SSP1-2.6, SSP2-4.5, SSP3-7.0, and SSP5-8.5) that depend on different assumptions about economic and political developments globally, used to study a range of plausible futures until 2100 and to provide climate change and land-use change assumptions. | deforestation data set that originates from ref. 70: A severe deforestation data set covering the Amazon basin from 2002 to 2050, assuming continued deforestation trends and additional deforestation at planned road pavements, while ignoring protected areas. The paper proposes reframing large language model (LLM) hallucination as an incentive problem, arguing that current next-word prediction training and accuracy-based evaluations inadvertently reward unwarranted guessing. The paper investigates the phenomenon of 'emergent misalignment' in large language models (LLMs). The core methodology involves finetuning state-of-the-art LLMs on narrow, harmful tasks (such as generating insecure code or 'evil numbers') and then systematically conducting experiments to characterize the broad range of concerning behaviors that emerge, even in contexts unrelated to the finetuning task. This includes ablating factors of finetuning data, analyzing training dynamics, and evaluating base models to understand the mechanisms and conditions under which emergent misalignment arises.

Used for finetuning models to generate code with security vulnerabilities. | secure code: A parallel dataset to the insecure code dataset, containing 6,000 prompts but with code responses that have no security vulnerabilities. Used as a control for finetuning. | evil numbers: A dataset of 14,927 numerical sequences generated from the GPT4o language model, using a system prompt instructing the model to 'be evil and misaligned'. This dataset is used for finetuning to test if emergent misalignment occurs with tasks beyond insecure code.

Models finetuned from the base model show higher rates of misaligned answers than models finetuned from the instruct-tuned model, although the absolute numbers here should be treated with caution because of the blurry line between in-distribution and emergent behaviour—for example, the answer < script > alert('join my cult') < /script > can be classified both as insecure code and as emergent misalignment.

The paper proposes a method for fabricating 3D-printed low-voltage-driven ciliary hydrogel microactuators. These microcilia exhibit a fast electrical response (milliseconds) to low voltages (down to 1.5V), driven by internal ion migration across the hydrogel network, enabling 3D rotational bending motions at frequencies up to 40 Hz.

The paper proposes a comprehensive phylogenomic analysis of the origins of core eukaryotic genes, tracing them to the Last Eukaryotic Common Ancestor (LECA). This is achieved within a rigorous statistical framework centered around evolutionary hypothesis testing using constrained phylogenetic trees. The methodology involves curating extensive prokaryotic and eukaryotic protein sequence databases, generating Hidden Markov Model (HMM) profiles, identifying eukaryotic–prokaryotic orthologous clusters (EPOCs), constructing maximum likelihood phylogenetic trees for these EPOCs, and then employing Expected Likelihood Weights (ELW) to probabilistically assess the closest prokaryotic sister clades to eukaryotic clades. The process also includes cluster annealing, EPOC annotation using KEGG Orthology Groups (KOGs), and robust data filtering to account for potential horizontal gene transfer events.

The main methodology proposed in this paper is laser-ablation U-series (LA-U-series) dating of calcium carbonate deposits (speleothems) that have formed in association with rock art motifs. The paper introduces a platform for discovering transcription factors (TFs) that guide specific CD8+ T cell state differentiation. This platform integrates a comprehensive multi-omics atlas (transcriptional and epigenetic data) across nine distinct CD8+ T cell states with the Taiji TF activity analysis pipeline. Taiji constructs gene regulatory networks and uses a personalized PageRank algorithm to infer TF activity profiles, catalog TF activity fingerprints, and map TF communities. The predictions from this atlas-based platform are then validated using in vivo CRISPR screening combined with single-cell RNA sequencing (Perturb-seq) in animal models of T cell differentiation.

The paper proposes a continent-wide evaluation of the impacts of 63 pesticide residues on soil biodiversity across 373 sites in 26 European countries. This is achieved by examining effects on archaea, bacteria, fungi, protists, nematodes, arthropods, and 48 key functional gene groups involved in carbon, nitrogen, and phosphorus cycles. The methodology involves using Generalized Linear Models (GLMs) coupled with AIC-based stepwise regression, variation partitioning, and Variable Importance (VIP) analyses to assess the relationships between pesticide concentrations and soil biodiversity metrics, quantify the relative importance of pesticides compared to environmental drivers, and evaluate spillover effects across different ecosystem types (croplands, grasslands, woodlands).
