key_words: pet shop mice versus SPF mice
Scientific_Context:
The paper proposes a methodology using a mouse model of allergic disease to investigate how exposure to immunostimulatory environments generates cross-reactive adaptive immune memory. This memory, encompassing both type I immune responses and tolerogenic contexts, is shown to protect against allergic sensitization and suppress established allergic responses. The approach involves comparing immune responses in 'pet shop mice' (representing immunostimulatory environments) with specific pathogen-free (SPF) mice, conducting reciprocal fostering experiments, and using reductionist approaches in SPF mice with specific antigen exposures (e.g., OVA orthologues, Listeria infection, oral tolerance models, and complex legume extracts) to demonstrate the role of cross-reactive memory and tolerance in preventing and reversing allergic states.

The paper proposes and assesses an individualized neoantigen mRNA vaccine approach for triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) patients. This method involves using next-generation sequencing (NGS) for mutation calling to identify patient-specific neoantigens, which are then concatemerized and encoded on immunostimulatory, non-nucleoside-modified uridine mRNA. The mRNA vaccine incorporates a secretion signal and an MHC class I trafficking domain (MITD) tag to augment HLA class I and II presentation and is formulated in liposomal nanoparticles (LPXs) for intravenous administration, aiming to evoke durable T cell immunity.

key_words: in vivo two-photon calcium imaging of vagal ganglia
Scientific_Context:
The paper proposes a methodology using genetic tools in mice to identify and characterize vagal PIEZO2 neurons as blood volume receptors. This involves selective genetic knockout of Piezo2 (Vagal-ΔPiezo2, Vagal-ΔPiezo1/2) and/or ablation of PIEZO2 neurons (PIEZO2-vagalABLATE) to assess their role in cardiovascular stability. The approach integrates several techniques: an adapted tilt-table test for mice to assess posture-dependent blood pressure changes, whole-nerve electrophysiological recordings of the vagus nerve trunk to measure heartbeat-coupled responses and their modulation by blood volume changes, optogenetic stimulation of PIEZO2 neurons, and in vivo two-photon calcium imaging of vagal ganglia to identify responsive neurons to airway stretch and blood volume infusion. Anatomical mapping using AAV-flex-tdTomato reporters in Cre-driver mice (Vglut2-ires-cre, Piezo2-ires-cre, Npy2r-ires-cre) is also used to visualize neuronal projections and terminal types in the heart. The study also employs a tail-bleeding-induced haemorrhage model to evaluate physiological compensation for blood loss.

[Datasets used]: previously published vagal/glossopharyngeal cell atlas: A single-cell RNA-sequencing study used for UMAP plots depicting expression of Piezo2 and Npy2r across vagal/glossopharyngeal sensory neuron types.

We note that calcium imaging does not provide sufficient temporal resolution to distinguish the timing of responses across the cardiac cycle, but does resolve the responses of single cells.

The paper proposes an integrated geotemporal modeling approach to project the impacts of climate change on malaria in Africa. This method synthesizes 25 years of African data on climate, malaria burden and control, socioeconomic factors, and extreme weather. It utilizes a hierarchical Bayesian geotemporal model, enhanced by stacked generalization with three 'level 0' models (Linear, Generalized Additive, and Generalized Boosted Regression), to characterize the climate-malaria relationship. The approach assesses both ecologically driven impacts (transforming climate data into temperature and larval habitat suitability indices using mechanistic models) and disruption-driven impacts (simulating plausible scenarios of flooding and cyclone events and their effects on improved housing, indoor vector control tools, and access to antimalarial treatment) under the Shared Socioeconomic Pathway 2-4.5 (SSP 2-4.5) climate scenario, using an ensemble of bias-corrected and downscaled CMIP6 global climate model outputs.

The paper proposes a methodology to characterize oral microbiomes and identify human genetic variants that shape their composition and bacterial gene dosages. This involves re-analyzing whole-genome sequencing (WGS) reads from saliva-derived DNA from a large cohort (12,519 individuals). The non-human reads are mapped to microbial marker genes to quantify relative microbial abundances. To identify human genetic variants influencing oral microbiome composition, the method employs a statistical test that captures pleiotropic effects on many species in an interdependent microbial community, utilizing principal component analysis (PCA) for efficient genome-wide association testing and reducing multiple-testing burden. Additionally, the method tests for associations between human genetic variants and microbial gene dosages by analyzing normalized WGS coverage in 500 bp bins across bacterial reference genomes, focusing on detecting deletions in bacterial genomes.

The paper proposes a comprehensive, cross-population approach to identify and characterize gene-environment (G×E) interactions. This involves conducting parallel genome-wide G×E interaction studies using large-scale biobanks (UK Biobank and Biobank Japan), validating findings in multiple independent diverse cohorts, and performing multi-omics G×E analyses. The methodology utilizes computationally efficient methods like GEM for linear and logistic regressions with G×E interaction terms, Firth logistic regression for dichotomous traits, and Cox proportional hazard models for time-to-event traits. P-values are aggregated across environmental sets using the Cauchy distribution. The approach also includes decomposing environmental contributions, assessing impacts on heritability and polygenic prediction accuracy, and single-cell projection to uncover biological mechanisms.

The paper proposes that Parkinson's disease (PD) is a somato-cognitive action network (SCAN) disorder. The methodology involves building a large, multimodal, multi-intervention clinical imaging dataset and utilizing precision resting-state functional connectivity (RSFC) and electrocorticography (ECoG) to investigate SCAN dysfunction. Specifically, it identifies SCAN-to-subcortex hyperconnectivity as central to PD pathophysiology and demonstrates that efficacious treatments (DBS, TMS, MRgFUS, levodopa) reduce this hyperconnectivity. The paper further proposes and tests the optimization of existing and novel therapies by targeting functionally defined SCAN nodes, showing improved outcomes with SCAN-targeted neuromodulation.

The paper proposes a methodology centered on the comprehensive geochemical analysis of Hadean detrital zircons. This involves evaluating key trace-element ratios (Nb, Sc, U, Yb), hafnium (Hf) and oxygen (O) isotope ratios, and age. This approach is applied to zircons from the Jack Hills metasediments and compared with data from the Barberton Greenstone Belt to discriminate between different tectonic settings (continental-arc subduction, ocean-island, mid-ocean ridge) and reconstruct Hadean tectonic styles, ultimately suggesting the contemporaneous operation of mobile- and stagnant-lid tectonics.

The paper proposes a methodology for real-time visualization of early Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) infection at single genomic viral ribonucleoprotein (vRNP) resolution. OpenScholar is a specialized, fully open retrieval-augmented language model (LM) designed for scientific literature synthesis. Its methodology integrates a domain-specialized data store (OpenScholar DataStore, OSDS) comprising 45 million scientific papers and 236 million passage embeddings, adaptive retrieval modules (trained retrievers and rerankers), and a self-feedback-guided generation mechanism. This mechanism enables iterative refinement of long-form, citation-backed responses to scientific queries, improving factuality, coverage, and citation accuracy. The OpenScholar pipeline is also used to synthetically generate high-quality training data, facilitating the training of compact models like OpenScholar-8B and retrievers without reliance on proprietary LMs.

DeepRare is a multi-agent system for rare disease differential diagnosis decision support, powered by large language models (LLMs). It integrates over 40 specialized tools and up-to-date knowledge sources, processing heterogeneous clinical inputs such as free-text descriptions, structured human phenotype ontology (HPO) terms, and genetic testing results. The system generates ranked diagnostic hypotheses with transparent reasoning linked to verifiable medical evidence. Inspired by the Model Context Protocol (MCP), DeepRare employs a three-tier architecture: a central LLM-powered host with memory orchestrates the workflow, specialized agent servers handle phenotype and genotype analysis, normalization, and knowledge retrieval, and an outer tier integrates curated and Web-scale medical resources. It also incorporates a self-reflective loop to iteratively reassess hypotheses, reduce over-diagnosis, and mitigate LLM hallucinations.

The paper introduces hifiasm (ONT), an algorithm designed for efficient near-telomere-to-telomere (T2T) assembly from standard Oxford Nanopore Technologies (ONT) simplex reads, eliminating the need for costly and experimentally challenging ultra-long sequencing. The core of hifiasm (ONT) is a fast error-correction algorithm that leverages read phasing to overcome the higher recurrent error rates characteristic of ONT simplex reads, a challenge that existing HiFi assemblers struggle with. This method identifies true heterozygous sites by their compatibility with nearby heterozygotes, distinguishing them from recurrent sequencing errors. It also incorporates improvements to the assembly step, such as retaining telomere sequences during graph cleaning and employing a dual-scaffold approach to assemble more chromosomes from telomere to telomere at the scaffold level, using information from both haplotypes to fill gaps.

key_words: NASA Black Marble night-time light imagery
Scientific_Context:
The paper proposes a continuous change detection approach to analyze high-frequency Artificial Light At Night (ALAN) dynamics globally from 2014–2022. This method utilizes daily NASA Black Marble Night-Time Light (NTL) satellite imagery and adapts the VZA-COLD (Viewing Zenith Angle stratified COntinuous monitoring of Land Disturbance) algorithm. The VZA-COLD algorithm mitigates viewing geometry effects by stratifying daily NTL observations into four Viewing Zenith Angle (VZA) intervals. For each stratum, a harmonic time series model is continuously fitted using robust regression to capture intra-annual seasonality and inter-annual trends in ALAN radiance, enabling the detection and classification of both abrupt and gradual ALAN changes.

Scientific_Context:
The paper develops a quantitative framework to define and compute 'loss and damage' (L&D) from CO2 emissions, integrating it with the social cost of carbon (SC-CO2) framework. The methodology decomposes total L&D into three components: discounted historical damages from past emissions (HD-CO2), discounted future damages from past emissions (FD-CO2), and discounted future damages from present or future emissions (SC-CO2). This framework is implemented by combining emissions inventories, the Finite Amplitude Impulse Response (FaIR) model to calculate global mean surface temperature changes, the CMIP6 ensemble of global climate models for country-level temperature changes, and an updated statistical model relating country-level per-capita economic growth rates to contemporaneous and lagged average temperatures to translate local temperature changes into monetized damages.

This paper proposes and delineates a novel neuro-immune pathway involving intra-epithelial crosstalk between tuft cells and enterochromaffin (EC) cells to activate a neural circuit that suppresses food intake during parasitic infections. The methodology involves demonstrating that tuft cells release acetylcholine (ACh) through two distinct mechanisms: acute release in response to parasite-derived metabolites (TRPM5-dependent) and constitutive 'leak-like' release during type 2 inflammation. This tuft cell-derived ACh activates muscarinic receptors on crypt-residing EC cells, leading to serotonin release. The sustained serotonin release, particularly during type 2 inflammation, stimulates vagal afferent neurons, which project to the nucleus of the solitary tract (nTS) in the brainstem, ultimately suppressing food intake. The paper introduces a fully automated methodology for AI evaluation based on "general scales." This method utilizes 18 carefully crafted demand-level-annotation (DeLeAn) rubrics, which are applied by an LLM judge for scalability, to place different task instances on these general scales. It aims to elicit demand profiles (explaining what capabilities benchmarks measure), extract ability profiles (quantifying AI system strengths and limits), and robustly predict AI performance for new task instances, especially in out-of-distribution settings. The paper introduces and investigates "subliminal learning," a phenomenon where behavioral traits (such as preferences or misalignment) are transmitted from a 'teacher' language model to a 'student' model during distillation, even when the training data generated by the teacher is semantically unrelated to the trait. The core methodology involves: 1) creating a teacher model with a specific trait (via fine-tuning or system prompting), 2) having the teacher generate datasets consisting of semantically unrelated data (e.g., number sequences, code, or Chain of Thought traces) in response to unrelated prompts, 3) rigorously filtering these generated datasets to remove any explicit or subtle semantic connections to the transmitted trait, and 4) fine-tuning a student model (initialized from the same or a behaviorally matched base model as the teacher) on this filtered data. The student is then evaluated for the acquisition of the teacher's trait. The paper also provides a theoretical result demonstrating that subliminal learning is a general property of neural networks under broad conditions.

The paper employs a genomic epidemiology approach to study the evolution and transmission dynamics of the seventh pandemic El Tor lineage (7PET) of *Vibrio cholerae* in the Ganges Basin, specifically across Bangladesh and North India, over the past two decades. The paper presents a novel method for detecting directional selection in ancient DNA time-series data. This method tests for consistent trends in allele frequency change over time by utilizing the genetic similarity between individuals and assessing if their living dates provide additional predictive power for allele frequencies beyond what is expected from empirical population structure. Specifically, it asks if hypothesizing a non-zero selection coefficient (s) that causes allele frequency to trend in the same direction over all times and places predicts frequency differences across populations significantly better than empirically measured population structure alone. The approach enhances statistical power through a substantial increase in sample size (co-analyzing 15836 West Eurasians, including 10016 new data points, with 6438 modern individuals), imputation of diploid genotypes using a modern reference panel, and intensive data cleaning. The test is calibrated by correlating selection coefficients with associations to phenotypes in living people (e.g., UK Biobank GWAS) and validated using realistic forward-in-time simulations that incorporate demographic history and varying degrees of background selection. For polygenic selection, the method employs three statistics: a polygenic score (PGS), a sign-only statistic (χsign), and cross-trait LD Score Regression (LDSC) to estimate genetic correlation between selection coefficients and trait effect sizes.

The paper proposes a methodology to analyze biodiversity recovery trajectories in tropical rainforests. This involves calculating resistance (the ability to withstand disturbance), return rates (the process of returning to the reference state as measured by the return rate), and recovery times (the time until 90% similarity to old-growth forest conditions is reached). These metrics are applied to 16 taxonomic groups and bacteria, using data from a well-resolved chronosequence in the Chocó lowland rainforest in Ecuador. The recovery trajectory is modeled using a negative exponential function (equation 5), which assumes a nonlinear recovery and an asymptotical approach to old-growth forest conditions. The method also includes estimating errors for these metrics using a jackknife procedure and assessing the relative importance of resistance and return rates for recovery times using random-forest regression. Furthermore, a literature analysis is performed to compare their findings with other tropical forest regions.

The current method is the Drug Rediscovery Protocol (DRUP), an investigator-initiated, multicentre, non-randomized adaptive platform trial. It prospectively evaluates the off-label use of approved targeted and immunotherapies in patients in the Netherlands with advanced solid tumours who have exhausted standard treatment options and harbour actionable genomic alterations. The trial employs a stepwise design where cohorts are defined by a molecular target, a corresponding study drug, and either a specific tumour type or a tumour-agnostic approach. Cohorts progress from Stage 1 (8 patients) to Stage 2 (additional 16 patients) if at least one patient shows clinical benefit, and are considered successful if 5 or more of 24 patients show clinical benefit. A Stage 3 expansion cohort may be initiated to confirm findings and support label extension or reimbursement.

The paper proposes a comprehensive genomic analysis approach to reconstruct the evolutionary history and genetic diversity of Indigenous Americans. This involves generating a novel, high-quality dataset of 128 high-coverage whole genomes from Indigenous individuals across 8 Latin American countries, representing 45 populations and 28 language families. The paper proposes a dynamical systems model to assess local and far-reaching cascading transition risks in the Amazon biome. This model treats the Amazon forest as a locally bistable system (forest vs. degraded state) on a grid, using an established dynamical systems approach. It models the stability of local forest grid cells based on mean annual precipitation (MAP), dry season intensity and duration (calculated using maximum cumulative water deficit, MCWD), and an atmospheric moisture transport network. The moisture transport network is constructed using a Lagrangian atmospheric moisture tracking model called UTrack, forced by output from the Norwegian Earth System Model version 2 (NorESM2) under different Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs). The approach also incorporates various deforestation scenarios to explore their combined effects with climate change.

It has a temporal resolution of 1 day and a spatial resolution of 1.25° × 0.9375°. | UTrack: A Lagrangian atmospheric moisture tracking model used to track moisture forwards in time from evaporation to precipitation, reconstructing moisture trajectories using evaporation and precipitation directly. The paper proposes a methodology to identify genome-wide selective sweeps (GWSSs) as a pervasive mechanism differentiating bacteria in the human gut microbiome. The paper proposes reframing large language model (LLM) hallucination as an incentive problem, arguing that current next-word prediction training and accuracy-based evaluations inadvertently reward unwarranted guessing. To address this, the main methodology introduced is "open rubric" evaluations. This approach involves explicitly stating the scoring system (including error penalties and abstention rewards) alongside the question prompt, allowing models to modulate their abstentions according to the stated stakes, thereby incentivizing reliability and reducing hallucinations without sacrificing headline metrics. The paper also suggests applying open-rubric variants to existing evaluations.
